1.title: Starting Up a Project in Context
1.text: Welcome to Module ten: Starting Up a Project in Context. It covers the exam area The prince two processes. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. four point one.one carry out starting up a project: activities, inputs and outputs. Recommended roles and responsibilities. How the practices are applied. four point one.two analyze whether the activities, roles and responsibilities are effective and fit for purpose, using the purpose and objectives, the practices and tailoring. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two processes (thirty percent). Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and context
1.text: Purpose, objectives and context. The starting up a project process makes sure the prerequisites for initiation are in place. It answers one question: do we have a viable and worthwhile project? It is deliberately short. It happens before the project proper and ends with a decision by the project board.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and context, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and context. The figure shows this: Starting up a project: the trigger or project mandate goes in, and the project brief, the initiation stage plan and the appointed roles come out for the board decision to authorize initiation.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and context, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and context. In plain words, the objectives are. A reason to do the project, shown in an outline business case. The executive and project manager appointed, and the project management team designed. Lessons from earlier work reviewed. A delivery approach chosen, and a project brief that gives the board enough to decide. The initiation stage planned. The process serves ensure continued business justification (the outline case), learn from experience (previous lessons), define roles, responsibilities and relationships (the team), manage by stages (the board authorizes the initiation stage first) and tailor to suit the project. Exam tip: Starting up asks "is it worth initiating?", not "how will we deliver everything?" It needs an outline business case and a plan for the initiation stage only.

1.title: Activities, inputs and outputs
1.text: Activities, inputs and outputs. Activity names below are given in general terms. The Official Book's wording may differ slightly, so learn what each activity achieves. Appoint the executive and the project manager. The people who lead are named, so accountability exists from the start. Capture previous lessons. Lessons from similar work are reviewed and the lessons log is started. Design and appoint the project management team. Business, user and supplier interests are represented; board, assurance and support roles are identified. Prepare the outline business case. The reason, expected benefits, rough cost and time, and options, in outline.

1.title: Activities, inputs and outputs, continued
1.text: Activities, inputs and outputs. Select the project approach and assemble the project brief. The way of delivering, such as linear, iterative or hybrid, and the brief for the board. Plan the initiation stage. The initiation stage plan: the work to produce the P I D, with cost, time and tolerances.

1.title: Activities, inputs and outputs, continued
1.text: Activities, inputs and outputs. Inputs. The trigger or project mandate; lessons from earlier projects; corporate standards and guidance; programme information, if any. Outputs. The project brief with the outline business case; the initiation stage plan; the appointed roles; a started project log; the request for the board to authorize initiation. Exam tip: The outputs of starting up are the project brief and the initiation stage plan. The P I D is not one of them; it is produced in initiating. If an option has a detailed baseline in start-up, it belongs to initiating.

1.title: Roles and responsibilities
1.text: Roles and responsibilities. The Official Book gives a table of who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each activity (the racy table). Responsible means does the work. Accountable means answers for the result. Consulted gives input. Informed is told. Learn each role's focus and check the book's table.

1.title: Roles and responsibilities, continued
1.text: Roles and responsibilities. Corporate or programme management. Provides the trigger or project mandate; makes sure the executive is appointed. Executive. Accountable for the outline business case and for getting the right team in place. Senior user. Brings the user need, and confirms users can commit people and time. Senior supplier. Brings the supplier view of the approach and what can be delivered.

1.title: Roles and responsibilities, continued
1.text: Roles and responsibilities. Project manager. Does much of the work: captures lessons, drafts the brief, plans the initiation stage, helps design the team. Project assurance. Independently checks the brief and the proposed team. Project support. Sets up the project log, filing and records. Exam tip: Doing the work is not the same as being accountable. The project manager may draft the outline business case, but the executive is accountable for it.

1.title: How the practices are applied
1.text: How the practices are applied. Business case. The outline business case in the project brief: reason, benefits, options. Organization. The executive and project manager are appointed; the team is designed to cover all three interests. Plans. The initiation stage plan; the project approach; an outline of the project product. Quality. The customer's quality expectations and acceptance criteria are noted in the brief. Risk. First risks and the risk appetite are noted; the risk register is started. Issues. Early issues are captured; the issue register is started. Progress. Tolerances for the initiation stage; the daily log and lessons log are started. Exam tip: In start-up each practice is applied lightly and in outline. Detailed approaches, a full plan and a final business case belong to initiating.

1.title: Judging the process
1.text: Judging the process. An executive with real authority, budget and time. A junior or unavailable executive (define roles). A team that covers the business, user and supplier interests. Only the supplier is represented; no senior user (define roles). Previous lessons reviewed and used. Lessons ignored because "this project is unique" (learn from experience). An outline business case that is honest and enough to decide. No case at all, or a detailed case that is really initiating work (business justification).

1.title: Judging the process, continued
1.text: Judging the process. A brief and initiation stage plan that are short and clear. Design or buying starts before the board authorizes initiation (manage by stages). Initiation tolerances agreed with the board. The project manager carries on with no stage tolerance (manage by exception). Project manager independent of assurance. Project manager also assures their own work (define roles).

2.title: Judging the process, continued
2.text: Judging the process. Tailoring scales the process, but does not remove it. Small internal project. A two-page brief and a short initiation stage plan; one meeting to authorize initiation. Agile or hybrid delivery. The approach names the iteration pattern and who speaks for users; the brief stays outline. Project in a programme. The mandate comes from the programme and the brief reuses its information. Sustainability concerns. Sustainability aims are noted in the outline business case. Exam tip: Tailoring shortens start-up but never skips the decision. A small project still needs a justified reason, a named executive and a board decision to initiate.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Before the board decides on initiation of Project Harbor, Sam Okafor, the project manager, produces detailed estimates, a full risk analysis and the quality management approach. Was this an appropriate action, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because start-up needs only an outline business case and an initiation stage plan. Starting up needs just enough information for the board to decide on initiation, while detailed approaches and estimates are produced in initiating.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Sam Okafor drafted the outline business case for Project Harbor from the project mandate. Who is accountable for the outline business case? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: The executive, Marta Quinn. The executive is accountable for the business case, even when the project manager does much of the drafting.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. While capturing lessons for Project Harbor, Sam finds that a permit project at another port overran because users were engaged too late. What should Sam do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Record the lesson in the lessons log and use it to shape the team and the approach. Capturing previous lessons is a start-up activity, and applying them to the team design and approach is the learn from experience principle in action.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Marta Quinn wants the board to decide whether to authorize initiation of Project Harbor. Which management product gives the board the outline business case, the project approach and the proposed team? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: The project brief, which holds the outline business case, the approach and the team. The project brief is the start-up output that lets the board decide on initiation, while the P I D is produced during initiating.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A small internal Brightwater project to replace staff laptops has one user group. Sam used a two-page project brief and a short initiation stage plan, and one board meeting authorized initiation. Was this an appropriate action, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Yes, because the process was scaled down but the board still had a justified case. Tailoring scales start-up down, but the board still needs a justified reason and a plan for initiation to decide on.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. For Project Harbor, Sam's draft team has Marta Quinn, Lena Kovac and a user representative who has no authority over harbor operations. What should Sam do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Propose Tomas Reyes, the harbor master, as a senior user able to commit users. The senior user must speak for the user interest with authority to commit people and decide, as Tomas Reyes does for harbor operations.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What question does starting up a project answer? Answer: Do we have a viable and worthwhile project? Question two. What is the trigger for starting up a project? Answer: The project mandate or trigger from the corporate, programme or customer level. Question three. Name the two main outputs. Answer: The project brief and the initiation stage plan.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which business case exists after starting up? Answer: The outline business case, held in the project brief. Question five. In a responsibility table, what does accountable mean? Answer: Answers for the result of the activity. Question six. Which log is started in start-up to hold earlier and new lessons? Answer: The lessons log.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Purpose: prerequisites for initiation; a viable and worthwhile project? Inputs: trigger or project mandate, earlier lessons, standards. Outputs: project brief, initiation stage plan, appointed roles. Activities: appoint, learn, design the team, outline case, approach and brief, plan initiation. Accountability: the executive for the case; the project manager does much of the work. Practices: applied lightly and in outline. Red flags: weak executive, missing interest, detailed work too early.
